section.title: The Man with the Measuring Line
section.sectionRationale: The third night vision, followed by a joyful oracle. A man goes to measure Jerusalem, but the word comes that the city will overflow its walls; God Himself will be a wall of fire around it and the glory within it. The vision then opens outward: exiles are called to flee Babylon, the nations will be judged, many will join themselves to the LORD, and He will come to dwell among His people.
section.thesis: God's restored city cannot be contained by walls, for He Himself is her wall of fire and her glory; He will judge those who harmed her, gather the nations to Himself, and come to dwell in her midst.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the measuring line and the promise of a city too full for walls; the wall of fire and the call to flee Babylon, for whoever touches Zion touches the apple of God's eye; and the joyful promise that God will dwell among His people and many nations will join the LORD.

verses.text: Then I lifted up my eyes and saw a man with a {{qav|measuring line}} in his hand.
“Where are you going?” I asked. “To measure Jerusalem,” he replied, “and to determine its width and length.”
Then the angel who was speaking with me went forth, and another angel came forward to meet him
and said to him, “Run and tell that young man: ‘Jerusalem will be a city without walls because of the multitude of men and livestock within it.
For I will be a wall of fire around it, declares the LORD, and I will be the {{kavod|glory}} within it.’”
“Get up! Get up! Flee from the land of the north,” declares the LORD, “for I have scattered you like the four winds of heaven,” declares the LORD.
“Get up, O Zion! Escape, you who dwell with the Daughter of Babylon!”
For this is what the LORD of Hosts says: “After His Glory has sent Me against the nations that have plundered you, for whoever touches you touches the {{babah|apple}} of His eye,
I will surely wave My hand over them, so that they will become plunder for their own servants. Then you will know that the LORD of Hosts has sent Me.”

units.label: God will dwell among you
units.note: many nations joined to the LORD

verses.text: “Shout for joy and be glad, O Daughter of Zion, for I am coming to {{shakan|dwell}} among you,” declares the LORD.
“On that day many nations will join themselves to the LORD, and they will become My people. I will dwell among you, and you will know that the LORD of Hosts has sent Me to you.
And the LORD will take possession of Judah as His portion in the Holy Land, and He will once again choose Jerusalem.
Be silent before the LORD, all people, for He has roused Himself from His holy dwelling.”

qav.gloss: A measuring line or cord, used to lay out the dimensions of a building or city. In 1:16 a measuring line over Jerusalem signaled restoration; here the young surveyor's line is gently overruled, because the coming city will be too full of people to be bounded by measured walls.

kavod.gloss: Glory, weight, honor, the visible radiance of God's presence that once filled the tabernacle and temple. God promises to be the glory within Jerusalem, her true protection and splendor, greater than any wall or building. This glory is fulfilled when the Word dwells among us in Christ.

babah.gloss: The pupil, the gate or little one of the eye, the most tender and fiercely guarded part of the body. To say that whoever touches God's people touches the apple of His eye is to declare how precious and protected they are; an attack on them is felt by God as an attack on Himself.

shakan.gloss: To dwell, settle, take up residence. It is the word behind the tabernacle and the later term Shekinah, the dwelling presence of God. God's promise to shakan among His people is the heart of the covenant, fulfilled when God dwells with us in Christ and consummated when He dwells with humanity forever.

basic.context: This is the third night vision, and the most joyful so far. A young man sets out to measure Jerusalem, but God stops the survey: the restored city will be so full of people that walls could never contain it. Instead God Himself will be its wall of fire and its glory. The vision then calls exiles still in Babylon to come home and promises that God will dwell among His people and draw in the nations.
basic.hermeneutics: This is vision plus oracle, so we read it for its promise rather than as a building plan. People ask how much refers to the second temple period and how much looks ahead to the last days when nations stream to God. The best answer is both: it begins to come true then and reaches its fullness in Christ and the new Jerusalem.
basic.originalLanguages: The man carries a qav, a measuring line, but the city will outgrow it. God promises to be the kavod, the glory, within Jerusalem. His people are the babah, the apple or pupil of His eye, fiercely guarded. And He pledges to shakan, to dwell, among them, the covenant word behind tabernacle and Shekinah.
basic.typology: God as the glory within Jerusalem points to Christ, in whom the glory of God dwells bodily. God coming to dwell among His people is fulfilled when the Word becomes flesh and tabernacles with us, and finally when God dwells with humanity in the new creation. The gathering of many nations foreshadows the church.
basic.christ: I am coming to dwell among you is answered supremely in Jesus, Immanuel, in whom God dwells with us. He is the glory of God, and through Him many nations are joined to the LORD and become His people. The city too full for walls is the growing people of God drawn from every nation.
basic.god: God is the true security and splendor of His people, better than any wall. He counts them as precious as the pupil of His own eye and takes their afflictions personally. He is holy and sovereign, roused from His dwelling to act, yet He delights to come near and dwell among the humble.
basic.crossReferences: John 1 says the Word dwelt among us and we beheld His glory. Revelation 21 shows the new Jerusalem without a temple, for God is its glory, and nations walk in its light. Deuteronomy 32 calls Israel the apple of His eye. Isaiah 2 and 60 foretell nations streaming to Zion.
basic.oneStory: The third vision opens the story outward: God's city cannot be contained, for He is her wall and glory, and He is coming to dwell among a people gathered from all nations. This runs straight to Christ, God dwelling with us, and on to the new Jerusalem where God dwells with humanity forever.

context.literary:
This is the third of the eight night visions, and it answers the promise that closed the first. In Zechariah 1:16 the LORD said that a measuring line would be stretched over Jerusalem, and in 1:17 that His cities would again overflow with prosperity. Here a man sets out with the line, and the vision shows what overflowing means: the city grows past the very tool brought to size it. The Hebrew Bible counts the first four verses of English chapter 2 as the end of chapter 1, so in the Hebrew text this vision opens a new chapter at what English readers number 2:5.

The passage widens in rings. The vision itself concerns one city (verses 1 to 5). The oracle that follows turns to the scattered people in Babylon (verses 6 and 7), then to the nations that plundered them (verses 8 and 9), then to the nations that will be joined to the LORD (verse 11), and it ends with a command to 'all people' (verse 13), which in Hebrew is the phrase 'all flesh'. The scope moves from a town to the whole human race, and the single hush at the end is the proper response to a plan that large.

Speakers pass the message along like a relay. Zechariah asks the surveyor; the interpreting angel goes out; a second angel meets him and gives the word to be carried to 'that young man'; then the LORD speaks directly, and a figure who is both sent by the LORD of Hosts and speaks as the LORD takes over in verses 8 to 11. The refrain 'declares the LORD' falls four times in verses 5 to 10, each time at a hinge: the promise of fire, the call to flee, and the promise of dwelling.

The vision also pairs with the sixth. In 2:2 the dimensions are 'width and length'; in 5:2 the scroll is given as length and width. One passage is about a city too full to measure, the other about a land measured by a curse, and the two frame the visions in between.
context.historical:
The vision is dated to the night of the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month in Darius's second year, about February 519 BC (Zechariah 1:7). Eighteen years earlier Cyrus had authorised a return and the rebuilding of the house of the LORD (Ezra 1:2 and 1:3). Construction had then stalled until Haggai and Zechariah stirred Zerubbabel and Jeshua to start again (Ezra 4:24 and 5:1 and 5:2). The empire had only just come through the revolts that followed Darius's accession, and the horsemen of the first vision had reported the earth 'at rest' (Zechariah 1:11), so there was little confidence that a small province on the Syrian road would be left alone.

Jerusalem was thinly settled and unwalled. Even in Nehemiah's day, more than seventy years later, the city was 'large and spacious, but there were few people in it' (Nehemiah 7:4), and the people had to cast lots to bring one in ten to live there (Nehemiah 11:1). A man with a measuring line therefore had a real task in mind: to plan walls the community could defend. In the ancient world a wall was the city's identity as well as its protection, and a city without one was exposed.

The call to 'flee from the land of the north' addresses people who had stayed in Babylon. The north is named because invasions from Mesopotamia came down the Syrian road (Jeremiah 1:14). Jeremiah had told earlier exiles to build houses and seek the city's welfare (Jeremiah 29:5 to 7), and many had taken him at his word and prospered. Isaiah 52:11 and Jeremiah 51:6 had already summoned them out. Zechariah repeats the summons to a second generation for whom Babylon was home and Zion was a story.
context.canonical:
The central promise, 'I am coming to dwell among you,' is the thread that runs from the tabernacle to the new creation. It is the purpose stated at Sinai, 'make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them' (Exodus 25:8). The thread breaks when Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD rise 'from within the city' and stand over the mountain to the east (Ezekiel 11:23). Ezekiel then watches it return by the same eastern gate and fill the temple (Ezekiel 43:2 to 5). Zechariah 2:5 and 2:10 promise that return before the second temple has been finished, and Zechariah 8:3 repeats it: 'I will return to Zion and dwell in Jerusalem.'

The New Testament takes up the verb at its most personal. John says the Word 'dwelt among us' (John 1:14), choosing a word that evokes the tabernacle, and Matthew names Him 'God with us' (Matthew 1:23). Paul says believers are 'being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit' (Ephesians 2:22). Revelation closes the line with 'the dwelling place of God is with man' (Revelation 21:3), in a city where the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple and its gates are never shut (Revelation 21:22 and 21:25).

The ingathering of the nations also has deep roots: the promise to Abraham that all families of the earth would be blessed, Isaiah's picture of the nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD (Isaiah 2:2 and 2:3), and Isaiah 19:24 and 19:25, where Egypt and Assyria are named 'My people' and 'My handiwork'. Zechariah 8:20 to 23 returns to the theme. Paul tells Gentile believers they are 'no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens' (Ephesians 2:19), which is Zechariah 2:11 seen from the inside.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Zechariah's hearers had a surveyor's instinct. They looked at a small, unwalled town and asked how large a wall it could afford and how many people could be found to fill it. The vision does not scold that instinct so much as overturn its premise. The first thing the interpreting angel does is stop the survey, because the city's future is bigger than any plan they could draw and its safety does not rest on masonry.

The oracle that follows aims at two groups. To the comfortable exiles still in Babylon it says, in effect, that settling there is no longer the right answer, because the LORD is doing something in Jerusalem and they are invited to be part of it. To the struggling remnant in Judah it says that they are not an afterthought: they are the LORD's 'portion,' the place He has chosen again (2:12). The command to shout for joy (2:10) is part of the message. Joy is presented as the fitting reply to a promise, not as a mood to be conjured.

Finally, the author wants Israel to see itself differently in relation to the nations. They had been plundered by them and might have wished only to see them punished. Verses 8 and 9 grant the judgment; verse 11 goes further, and promises that many of those nations will be joined to the LORD and become His people. A community that expected its neighbours to be enemies for ever is told that its God has bigger designs.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The imperatives in the passage are addressed to particular people in 519 BC. 'Flee from the land of the north' was a summons to exiles to rejoin the community in Judah; it is not a general rule that believers must leave their cities or nations. The New Testament does take the language up in a spiritual sense, as when a voice from heaven says 'Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins' (Revelation 18:4), but there the call is to refuse the corruption of the world's systems, not to retreat from the world.

The wall of fire is a promise of what God's presence will be, not a prohibition on walls. Nehemiah later rebuilt them, with God's evident blessing, and finished the wall in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15). Prudence and trust sit together; what the vision forbids is putting ultimate trust in the wall.

'Whoever touches you touches the apple of His eye' states how the LORD regards His own people. It does not hand any modern nation or movement a blank cheque, and it must be read alongside verse 11, where the circle of 'My people' widens to include the nations. The way it carries forward is as comfort and warning: God takes the suffering of His people personally.

debates.question: Does the promise of an unwalled, overflowing city refer to the post-exilic period or the messianic age?

views.label: Ultimately the messianic and eternal age
views.case: The scale of the promise, many nations joined to the LORD and God dwelling in the midst, outruns anything the second temple period saw. Revelation 21 shows a city that is measured and walled, and yet whose gates are never shut and whose temple is God Himself, which is the fullness that Zechariah 2 points toward.

views.label: Beginning then and expanding toward the end
views.case: The promise genuinely encouraged the returning remnant and began to unfold in their day, as the temple was finished in 516 BC (Ezra 6:15) and the population slowly grew. It then widens through the gospel to its consummation, so that present and future are held together.

debates.bearing: Either way the hope is God's presence and the ingathering of the nations, realised in Christ; the debate concerns timing, not the substance of the promise.

debates.question: Who is the 'Me' sent against the nations in verses 8, 9 and 11?

views.label: The angel of the LORD, the divine messenger
views.case: The speaker is sent by the LORD of Hosts, yet speaks in the first person as the LORD: 'I will surely wave My hand over them' and 'I will dwell among you.' This matches the pattern in which the angel of the LORD is distinguished from the LORD and also identified with Him. Many Christian readers see here the Son sent by the Father.

views.label: The prophet or another commissioned agent
views.case: Prophets regularly speak in the first person for the LORD, and verse 11 says the nations will know that the LORD of Hosts has sent 'me,' as Zechariah says of himself in 4:9. On this reading the speaker is the prophet, whose word carries God's authority.

debates.bearing: Both readings keep the LORD as the one who initiates and guarantees the promise. Only the first explains why the sent one can say 'I will dwell among you' of a presence the LORD of Hosts has authorised, which is why the church has found the Son in this verse.

debates.question: Who is 'that young man' to whom the message is carried in verse 4?

views.label: The surveyor with the measuring line
views.case: The angel's command is 'Run and tell that young man,' and the last person mentioned is the man who had set out to measure. The message tells him that his errand is unnecessary.

views.label: Zechariah himself
views.case: Some think the angel means the prophet, who is the only other human in the scene and who must carry the message to the people. The Hebrew word is used of a youth or a junior servant, which would suit a young prophet.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle it. In both cases the content is to be passed on to the community, which is why the prophet records the word and does not keep it as a private revelation.

study.originalLanguages:
Four words and phrases the basic level does not take up show how carefully the passage is worded.

The 'city without walls' of verse 4 is built on a plural noun, perazot, which means unwalled settlements, open villages with no fortification. Ezekiel 38:11 uses the same term of 'a land of unwalled villages' that an invader despises as easy plunder. Zechariah turns the insult into a blessing: the city will sprawl across the countryside like a village, and its safety will be the LORD's presence and not an enclosure.

In verse 8 the clause translated 'After His Glory has sent Me' is genuinely hard. The BSB footnote offers two alternatives, 'After the Glorious One has sent Me' and 'After He has honored Me and sent Me.' The ambiguity matters, because in the first reading 'Glory' is a title for the LORD Himself, and the speaker is therefore someone sent by 'the Glory' who also speaks as God.

The 'apple of His eye' has a double background in the Hebrew Bible. Zechariah's noun is the rare babah, which the BSB footnote glosses as 'the pupil.' Deuteronomy 32:10 and Psalm 17:8 use a different word, ishon, which means literally a 'little man,' the tiny image of yourself you see in another person's eye. Both pictures say that the LORD holds His people at the centre of His gaze. Deuteronomy 32:9, the verse before, supplies the other half: 'the LORD's portion is His people.' Zechariah 2:12 says the LORD will take Judah 'as His portion,' so the two verses of Moses' song stand behind verses 8 and 12.

'Join themselves' in verse 11 is the verb lavah, 'to be attached.' It is the root of the name Levi, whom Leah hoped would make her husband 'attached' to her (Genesis 29:34), and Moses uses it for the Levites who will 'join' Aaron in serving at the tent (Numbers 18:2). Isaiah 56:6 uses it of foreigners who 'join themselves to the LORD to minister to Him.' The nations in Zechariah 2:11 are therefore being drawn into a priestly closeness.

Finally, the sudden call 'Be silent' in verse 13 uses the interjection has, the same word as Habakkuk 2:20 and Zephaniah 1:7. Both texts announce that God is about to act. Here He has 'roused Himself,' a verb from the root for waking or stirring, so the silence is the hush of a courtroom or a sickroom when the one who matters has just entered.

typology.type: A city too large for its walls, Zechariah 2:4
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah had already told Zion to 'enlarge the site of your tent' because her descendants would 'spread out to the right and left' (Isaiah 54:2 and 54:3). Paul takes that promise and applies it to 'the Jerusalem above,' our mother, whose children outnumber those of the one who has a husband (Galatians 4:26 and 4:27). The growth is therefore the church, drawn from every nation. The type falls short of the fullness: even in Revelation the city has walls and gates, though its gates are never shut, Revelation 21:25, so the end is a secure city and not an unbounded one.

typology.type: The wall of fire and the glory within, Zechariah 2:5
typology.fulfillment: The picture recalls the pillar of cloud and fire that stood between Israel and Egypt (Exodus 14:19 and 14:20) and the cloud and flame that Isaiah promised over Zion (Isaiah 4:5). At Pentecost 'tongues like flames of fire' came to rest on each of the disciples (Acts 2:3). The Gospels and Acts do not tie this to Zechariah by name, so it is an echo and not a declared fulfilment, but it fits: the protecting fire no longer circles a city but settles on the people who are the dwelling. The type falls short because the fire of Zechariah guards a place, while the Spirit now indwells persons.

typology.type: God coming to dwell in the midst, Zechariah 2:10
typology.fulfillment: The tabernacle and temple were the outward form of this promise, but both were buildings. John 1:14 says the Word 'dwelt among us,' and Jesus spoke of the temple of His body (John 2:19 to 21). After His ascension the dwelling extends to His people: they are 'being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit' (Ephesians 2:22). The escalation is from a house, to a person, to a people. The type will not be complete until the city of Revelation 21:3, in which God Himself is with them.

typology.type: The call to leave Babylon, Zechariah 2:6 and 2:7
typology.fulfillment: Babylon becomes the standing symbol of the world's proud, godless order. Paul quotes Isaiah's summons to leave Babylon when he tells the Corinthians to 'come out from among them and be separate' (2 Corinthians 6:17), and John hears the call again in Revelation 18:4. The escalation is that departure is no longer a journey over a road to a place, but a turning of allegiance wherever one lives. The type falls short in that a believer is sent into the world as well as called out of its ways.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first through its strange double voice. In verses 8 to 11 someone speaks who has been sent by 'the LORD of Hosts' and yet says 'I will wave My hand over them' and 'I will dwell among you.' The sender and the sent are both called the LORD. John's Gospel repeats the pattern constantly, with Jesus insisting that He has been sent and that the Father has sent Him (John 17:8), while also declaring that He and the Father are one. Isaiah 48:16 has the same shape: 'the Lord GOD has sent me, accompanied by His Spirit.' Care is needed here, since Zechariah does not give a doctrine of the Trinity. But it is no accident that the church read these verses and found the Son.

The promise of dwelling is answered by the incarnation. 'I am coming to dwell among you' becomes 'the Word became flesh and dwelt among us' (John 1:14), and the glory that Zechariah says will be 'within' the city is the glory John says 'we have seen.' The command 'Shout for joy... O Daughter of Zion' is taken up again in Zechariah 9:9, which Matthew applies to Jesus' entry into Jerusalem on a donkey (Matthew 21:5). The King who comes to Zion is the LORD who said, 'I am coming.'

The warning that 'whoever touches you touches the apple of His eye' finds its sharpest echo on the Damascus road. Saul had been dragging believers to prison, and the risen Christ asked, 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?' (Acts 9:4). Jesus identifies Himself with His people in the same way at the last judgment: 'whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me' (Matthew 25:40).

The measuring line also finds a fitting answer in Christ. The surveyor wanted the width and length of Jerusalem. Paul prays that believers will grasp 'the length and width and height and depth of the love of Christ' and know this love 'that surpasses knowledge' (Ephesians 3:18 and 3:19). The city that cannot be measured is held within a love that cannot be measured.

The nations are joined to the LORD through Him. Jesus tells His disciples to make disciples of all nations, and Paul explains that the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile has been removed in Christ (Ephesians 2:14). The risen Lord's promise 'I am with you always' (Matthew 28:20) is the same assurance of presence, offered to the nations.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The surveyor, the young man and the walls are not codes for individual persons or events in Jesus' life. The links above rest on the New Testament's own use of the themes of dwelling, glory, the sent one and the nations.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is that He is not satisfied to protect His people from a distance. He does not promise to post guards over Jerusalem; He promises to be the wall of fire around it and the glory within it. In the words of verse 10, 'I am coming to dwell among you.' When Moses asked that the LORD's presence go with Israel, he said it was this presence that distinguished them from all other peoples (Exodus 33:15 and 33:16). The vision restores that logic. Security and identity both come from who is in the midst.

God is also shown holding together things that are hard to hold together. He is the one whom 'even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain' (1 Kings 8:27), and yet He comes to live in a city that cannot be contained either. He rouses Himself 'from His holy dwelling' (verse 13), heaven, in order to come to a dwelling on earth (verse 10). The passage does not resolve this tension by shrinking God; the transcendent God chooses nearness, and the choice is the glory of it.

He is sovereign over the nations, and His sovereignty has two faces. Those who plundered His people will in turn become plunder, and the LORD will deal with them (verse 9). Yet in verse 11 many nations will join themselves to Him and become His people. The same God who judges is the God who gathers. Neither action is arbitrary; both come from His covenant faithfulness to the blessing promised through Abraham to all families of the earth.

He is passionate and tender about His own. 'Apple of His eye' speaks of a love that cannot bear to see its object hurt. Elsewhere Scripture says He will rejoice over Zion with singing (Zephaniah 3:17). A God who sings over His people is not distant. And He is faithful to His word: the measuring line promised in Zechariah 1:16 appears here, and the man who carries it is told that the promise is bigger than his plan.

The passage shapes worship in two directions. It commands shouting and gladness (verse 10), because the coming of God is news too good to receive quietly. It also commands the hush of verse 13, because the coming of God is also serious. A people who only shout may forget His holiness; a people who only hush may forget His kindness. Zechariah asks for both.

Finally, it teaches how God leads His people out of comfortable captivity. He does not drive them out with threats but draws them with a promise bigger than Babylon's comforts. His call to leave is a call to join Him.

crossReferences.note: The promise this vision unfolds. The LORD says He will return to Jerusalem with mercy and that a measuring line will be stretched over it; then He adds that His cities will again overflow with prosperity. Chapter 2 shows the two statements meeting: the line is brought, and the overflow is what makes it unnecessary.

Zion is told to enlarge her tent, lengthen her ropes and drive her stakes deep, because her descendants will spread out to the right and left. The same picture as Zechariah's unwalled city, but there an act of faith, here an action of promise. Paul quotes the next verse in Galatians 4:27.

Moses' song says the LORD's portion is His people and that He guarded Jacob as the apple of His eye. Zechariah 2:8 and 2:12 pick up both phrases together, so the post-exilic promise is anchored in the oldest statement of why Israel is precious to God.

The purpose of the tabernacle, in God's own words: 'make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them.' The verb for dwelling is the one Zechariah uses in 2:10 and 2:11, so the promise is that the original purpose of the sanctuary will be fully realised.

The glory of God returns from the east and enters the temple, reversing Ezekiel 11:23 where it left. Zechariah's 'I will be the glory within it' belongs to the same hope, spoken to a community still waiting for the return that Ezekiel saw in vision.

Decades after Zechariah the city was still 'large and spacious, but there were few people in it.' The comparison shows how bold Zechariah's promise of an overflowing city was in his own day, and why the vision is received as a work of God and not an extrapolation from the evidence.

The LORD will create 'a cloud of smoke by day and a glowing flame of fire by night' over Mount Zion, with a canopy over all the glory. Isaiah's canopy of fire and Zechariah's wall of fire are the same promise, drawing on the pillar of fire that led Israel from Egypt.

Foreigners who 'join themselves to the LORD to minister to Him' are welcomed in the same terms as Zechariah 2:11. Together they answer the fear that the nations could only be enemies, since both texts see them taking up the covenant as worshippers.

Zephaniah also calls Zion to sing and rejoice because 'the LORD your God is among you; He is mighty to save.' The command to joy and the promise of presence run together in both prophets, which suggests a settled pattern in post-exilic hope.

A voice from heaven says, 'Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins.' It reuses the call to leave Babylon, now for a symbolic city, and shows how the Old Testament summons keeps its force as a call to separate from the world's corruption.

Paul prays that believers will comprehend 'the length and width and height and depth of the love of Christ.' The dimensions that Zechariah's surveyor sought for a city are used by Paul for a love that exceeds knowledge, a fitting reply to the vision's stopped survey.

'The LORD is in His holy temple; let all the earth be silent before Him.' The same call to hush before God's holy dwelling appears in Zechariah 2:13, which suggests the later prophet is drawing on Habakkuk's image of the Lord about to act.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture begins with God dwelling with humanity. In Genesis 3:8 He walks in the garden in the cool of the day, and the first consequence of the fall is that the man and woman hide from Him and are driven east of Eden. Everything afterwards is the long work of bringing God and a human family back under one roof. The tabernacle (Exodus 25:8) and then the temple are the first answer, and they are partial, because only a few may enter and the holiness of the place keeps most people out.

Zechariah speaks at the low point of the second chapter of that story. The glory had departed the temple (Ezekiel 11:23), the city had been burned, the people scattered 'like the four winds,' and the rebuilt community was small. The vision answers these losses one by one. The measuring line is pushed aside because the city will be larger than the plan. The wall of fire answers the destroyed walls. The glory answers the departure of glory. The call to leave Babylon answers the scattering. The nations answer the old promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed.

What the vision sets up is the incarnation. 'I am coming to dwell among you' is promise in the future tense, and Matthew and John say it has happened: God with us, the Word dwelling, glory seen. Pentecost then puts that dwelling inside a people, who are called the temple of God, and the church grows as the unwalled city grows, one nation after another.

The story ends where the vision points. In the new creation the city is measured, as the angel measures with a golden rod in Revelation 21:15, and its dimensions are perfect and equal. Yet its gates are never shut, the nations walk by its light, there is no temple because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, and the dwelling place of God is with man. The surveyor's fear that there would not be enough room has been answered in the largest possible way: God has made room for the world.

quiz.q: Why will Jerusalem be a city without walls?

options.text: Because it will overflow with so many people and livestock, and God Himself will be its wall of fire.
options.note: Verses 4-5 promise a city too full for walls, protected by God's own presence.

options.text: Because the people will be too poor to build walls.
options.note: The absence of walls is a sign of abundance and divine protection, not poverty.

options.text: Because walls are forbidden in the Holy Land.
options.note: There is no such prohibition; the point is God's presence surpassing walls.

options.text: Because the city will be abandoned.
options.note: The city overflows with life, the opposite of abandonment.

quiz.q: What does it mean that whoever touches God's people touches the apple of His eye?

options.text: God counts His people as supremely precious and takes any attack on them as an attack on Himself.
options.note: The pupil of the eye is the most tender, fiercely guarded part; God guards His people so.

options.text: God is easily irritated by minor offenses.
options.note: The image is about preciousness and protection, not petty irritation.

options.text: God keeps His distance from His people's troubles.
options.note: The opposite: He feels their afflictions as His own.

options.text: God only protects the strongest among His people.
options.note: He guards all His people as the apple of His eye, not just the strong.

quiz.q: What is the climactic promise of this vision?

options.text: I am coming to dwell among you, with many nations joined to the LORD as His people.
options.note: Verses 10-11 promise God's dwelling presence and the ingathering of the nations.

options.text: That Jerusalem will finally get high stone walls.
options.note: The promise is God's presence surpassing walls, not stronger fortifications.

options.text: That the nations will be shut out forever.
options.note: Many nations will join themselves to the LORD, not be excluded.

options.text: That God will remain far off in heaven.
options.note: The promise is precisely that God will come to dwell among His people.

quiz.q: How is the promise God as the glory within it fulfilled in Christ?

options.text: In Jesus the glory of God dwells bodily, the Word made flesh who tabernacled among us.
options.note: John 1:14 and Colossians 2:9 show Christ as the glory of God dwelling with His people.

options.text: It is never fulfilled and remains only a wish.
options.note: The New Testament presents it as fulfilled in Christ and consummated in the new Jerusalem.

options.text: It refers only to gold decorating the temple.
options.note: The glory is God's own presence, not mere ornamentation.

options.text: It means God's glory left His people for good.
options.note: The promise is God's glory coming to dwell within, fulfilled in Christ.

quiz.q: Why are exiles told to flee from the land of the north?

options.text: God is calling His scattered people home to the restored city where He will dwell.
options.note: Verses 6-7 summon those still in Babylon to return to Zion.

options.text: Because the north was more comfortable and they should stay.
options.note: They are told to leave the comfort of Babylon, not remain in it.

options.text: Because God had permanently rejected them there.
options.note: God calls them back in love, not final rejection.

options.text: Because Jerusalem had been destroyed again.
options.note: Jerusalem is being restored, which is why they are called home.

questions: God promised to be a wall of fire around His people rather than relying on stone. Where are you tempted to trust in walls of your own making instead of God's presence?
God calls His people the apple of His eye. How does it change your sense of worth to know that God guards you as tenderly as the pupil of His own eye?
Exiles were told to get up and flee comfortable Babylon to come home. Is there a comfortable place God is calling you to leave in order to follow Him more fully?
The vision promises a city too full for walls, gathered from many nations. How does the worldwide scope of God's people enlarge your vision of the church?
I am coming to dwell among you is fulfilled in Christ, God with us. How does knowing God has come near, and will dwell with you forever, steady you today?

translationNotes.note: Glory renders kavod, the weighty radiance of God's presence; God promises to be Jerusalem's protection and splendor, language John applies to Christ dwelling among us.

Apple of His eye renders a phrase for the pupil, the most tender and guarded part of the eye; a footnote notes the alternative the pupil. The clause After His Glory has sent Me is difficult and variously rendered, as the footnote shows.
Dwell renders shakan, the covenant word behind the tabernacle and the later term Shekinah, the settled presence of God among His people.
